generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase FCC high-entropy CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy with a gradient or hierarchical grain structure, the local deformation mechanisms can be systematically tuned to achieve a stable plastic deformation response across a wide temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase CoCrFeMnNi alloy with homogeneous chemistry, processed into a gradient microstructure from submicrometer grains to coarse grains.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled thermal–mechanical processing (multi-step rolling and annealing) to produce a deliberate grain-size gradient within the CoCrFeMnNi material.
generation.conditions: Temperature range spanning cryogenic (~77 K) to elevated temperatures (up to ~900 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and dislocation structures formed by the gradient microstructure, providing sites for dislocation slip or twinning across different length scales.
generation.mechanism: The graded microstructure regulates temperature-dependent dislocation activities, promoting enhanced work-hardening at lower temperatures and stable plastic flow at higher temperatures by distributing slip, twinning, and boundary-mediated deformation among fine and coarse grains.
generation.predicted_outcome: Mechanically, the alloy sustains relatively high strength and ductility over a broad temperature range, with increased tolerance to plastic strain localization due to microstructural heterogeneity.
generation.baseline: Uniform CoCrFeMnNi generally shows consistent strength and ductility, but lacks the additional tuning of dislocation pathways afforded by grain-size gradients.
generation.boundary: Benefits may be diminished at extreme temperatures near or beyond 1000 °C or under rapid strain rates, where grain growth or phase evolution can reduce intended microstructural effects.
generation.uncertainty: The precise contribution of short-range ordering and twin-mediated deformation in different temperature regimes remains to be fully elucidated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three CoCrFeMnNi samples with varying controlled gradient grain structures, subject them to tensile tests from cryogenic to ~900 °C, and use in-situ or post-mortem microscopic methods to observe active deformation mechanisms in each gradient region.
measurements: Macroscopic stress–strain response over the temperature range
Post-deformation microstructural changes (grain refinement, twins, dislocation substructures)
Comparison of yield strength and ductility with uniform-grained reference samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the gradient structure does not result in distinct or improved plastic deformation behaviors compared to uniform-grained CoCrFeMnNi across the tested temperatures, the hypothesis is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] . decision.trend: Early studies (PMC4976365) on Al0.1CrCoFeNi (FCC-based) revealed distinct temperature-dependent stress responses in tension vs. compression from 77–1000 K, highlighting sensitivity to thermally activated dislocation processes. Follow-up work (PMC7514651) added small Mo/Hf to an Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni–Ti alloy to enhance high-temperature performance up to 900 °C, focusing mainly on strengthening but underscoring the importance of microstructural stability under heat. Subsequent investigations on CoCrFeMnNi (PMC7229066) noted consistently high strength and ductility from room temperature to 900 °C, establishing this alloy as a robust model system for studying thermally influenced deformation. In parallel, NbTaTiV (PMC11206460) and CoNiCrFeMn (PMC8357793) emphasized how BCC vs. FCC high-entropy alloys respond to rising temperatures via changes in dislocation type (edge vs. screw) and in deformation mechanisms (twining, short-range order). Overall, the trend moved from basic compositional exploration to targeted doping strategies and advanced characterization, culminating in recognition that controlling dislocation activity and phase stability across broad temperature windows remains key.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress in characterizing high-entropy alloys across wide temperature ranges, the interplay between short-range order, grain structure, and active deformation mechanisms is still incompletely understood. Optimizing microstructures for predictable plastic responses from cryogenic to high temperatures requires systematic tuning of grain architectures and deformation pathways, without defaulting to new composition changes.
decision.lever: Engineer a gradient or hierarchical grain structure in a stable single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) from submicron to coarse grains through controlled thermal–mechanical processing, ensuring uniform chemistry but spatially varied grain sizes and boundary densities to isolate and study local deformation modes.
decision.why: Prior work shows that dislocation transport, twinning, and short-range order vary with temperature and microstructure. A gradient microstructure in a well-characterized, compositionally uniform FCC HEA (such as CoCrFeMnNi) is the logical next step to decouple and systematically investigate how different grain sizes and boundary architectures govern plastic flow across a broad temperature range.
